title: Guardians Clinch Decisive ALDS Game 5 as White Sox Miss First ALCS Shot Since 2005
body:
CLEVELAND — The Guardians seized control of the American League Division Series on Thursday, blasting two fifth‑inning home runs to overturn the Chicago White Sox’s early lead and force a winner‑takes‑all Game 5 on Saturday. The dramatic swing not only erased a 2‑1 deficit but also underscored Cleveland’s resurgence after a decade‑long playoff drought, while Chicago’s hopes of reaching its first ALCS since 2005 slipped further away.

The game began with Chicago’s offense flashing early promise. After a quiet first inning, the White Sox struck in the second, loading the bases and delivering a two‑run single that put them ahead 2‑0. Pitcher Logan Allen, who had been solid in the early innings, settled in, and the Sox appeared poised to take a commanding 2‑0 lead into the later frames. However, the tide turned abruptly in the fifth inning when the Guardians’ power surged.

Cleveland’s right‑hander Triston McKenzie, who had been effective through four innings, surrendered a solo home run to Chicago’s Yoán Moncada, narrowing the gap to 2‑1. The Guardians responded instantly. After a routine strikeout, rookie outfielder Steven Kwan worked a full count before launching a towering solo shot to left‑center, tying the game at 2‑2. Moments later, veteran catcher Ryan McMahon followed with a second straight homer, pushing the Guardians ahead 3‑2. The sudden burst of offense left the White Sox scrambling and forced them to rely on their bullpen for the remainder of the night.

The shift in momentum was palpable. Chicago’s bullpen, anchored by reliever Liam Hendriks, struggled to contain Cleveland’s hitters, conceding two more runs in the seventh and eighth innings. The Guardians’ offense, which had been relatively muted through the first four innings, erupted for a total of five runs, while the White Sox managed only one additional run in the ninth, courtesy of a solo homer by Gavin Sheets that proved too little, too late. The final 5‑3 score sent Cleveland to the brink of a series victory and set the stage for a decisive fifth game.

Analysts point to several key factors behind Cleveland’s turnaround. First, the Guardians’ ability to adjust mid‑game, particularly in the fifth inning, demonstrated a level of strategic flexibility that had been missing in earlier postseason outings. Manager Stephen Vogt’s decision to keep McKenzie in the game longer paid dividends, as the veteran pitcher settled after the initial home run and delivered clutch outs thereafter. Second, the emergence of Kwan as a postseason threat cannot be overstated; his timely hitting and disciplined approach at the plate have become a hallmark of Cleveland’s recent success. Finally, Chicago’s reliance on a thin starting rotation—exacerbated by injuries to key arms—left the Sox vulnerable once their starter faltered, forcing an overtaxed bullpen to shoulder the load.

For the White Sox, the loss is a stark reminder of the challenges that have dogged the franchise since its last ALCS appearance in 2005. Despite a strong regular season that saw Chicago clinch a wild‑card berth, the team’s offensive inconsistency and bullpen depth were exposed in the high‑stakes environment of postseason baseball. Manager Pedro Grifol now faces the task of regrouping his roster, evaluating the effectiveness of his bullpen options, and perhaps reconsidering his lineup construction for the potential Game 5 showdown.

Looking ahead, Game 5 promises to be a high‑octane affair with everything on the line. Cleveland will aim to close out the series and advance to the American League Championship Series, where a matchup against either the Texas Rangers or the Houston Astros looms. Chicago, meanwhile, must summon a comeback effort that has only been witnessed a handful of times in MLB history. The stage is set for a climactic finale that could either cement the Guardians’ return to relevance or extend the White Sox’s postseason drought for another year.
